lessons.title: Unity UI builder
lessons.summary: Learn the basics of Unity UI
lessons.author: Alex Li

files.name: Font

figures.text: Create a new Canvas object in your inspector (Right click -> UI (Canvas) -> Canvas
UI operates in a different later than the scene, so we need to change some settings to easily edit it. Change the following settings on your Canvas object
Render mode: Screen Space - Camera
Render Camera: Main Camera
Order in layer: 32767
This will overlay your UI over your main world in the way you would see it in game.

figures.alt: The scene hierarchy after adding the player sprite

figures.text: We want our UI to work with screens of different sizes, so we also need to set some canvas scaling settings.
Set the following settings in your Canvas Scaler
UI Scale Mode: Scale with screen size
Screen match mode: Match width or height
Reference resolution: 1920x1080
Match: 0.5

figures.alt: The scene hierarchy after adding the player sprite

content.title: Testing with a constant aspect ratio

figures.text: The Unity testing window automatically resizes to whatever size is not taken up by your project, inspector, and hierarchy windows which can sometimes be a very strange aspect ratio. In order to test using an aspect ratio similar to what you will actually see on a computer screen, you can lock your aspect ratio at the top of the Game window. For this lesson, we will be using 16:9 as our standard size.

figures.alt: The scene hierarchy after adding the player sprite

figures.text: To add text to your scene, create a new text object under your Canvas (Right click > UI (Scene) > Text - TextMeshPro). The first time you do this, Unity will ask you to import TMP essentials, this is expected so just click to import them. You can edit the text position and size using an intuitive drag editor similar to Google Slides, and the text itself in the inspector.

The Unity default font is pretty boring and feels out of place, so let's add a custom pixel art font to our game. You can use the font attached at the top of this lesson or find your own font (TTF or OTF file). Drag the font into your Unity project to import it.

We need to turn this font file into something the Unity text understands. To do this, we can use the TextMeshPro Font Asset Creator. You can open this under Window > TextMeshPro -> Font Asset Creator. This will open a window similar to the tilemap editor.

Click on the little circle in the "Source Font" box and select your font, or drag your font into the box. For this lesson, we do not have to change the default settings, so click "Generate Font Atlas" and save the asset as a new font asset.
To use this font in your text, select it in the "Font asset" section of your text object.

Images work very similarly to sprites in the scene. Create an image in the Canvas (Right click > UI (Scene) > Image). You can assign a sprite texture to them and drag and resize it the same way as text.
Buttons are images with a text label and a click handler which can be used to easily create UI interactions. You can create a button in the scene using Right click > UI (Scene) > Button - TextMeshPro
For this lesson, we will use the provided circle sprite as a button sprite. In order to use this for the buttons, we need to configure some scaling settings in the sprite editor.

UI buttons can be many sizes, and it would take a long time to make a new sprite for every size, so we use a method called 9-slicing to automatically resize one sprite to work for any button size. To set up this scaling, open the sprite editor from the inspector and drag the green lines (which start on the edge of the sprite) until they are near the center of the sprite like the image shown. Then, click "Apply" to save your settings.
Now assign this sprite as your button's main sprite and try resizing your button. Instead of stretching, the button should scale as a square with rounded corners.

We can use button click events to make buttons perform actions. For the example in this lesson, we will need 2 buttons and one other image. For the two buttons, set them up as follows: Click the plus sign at the bottom of the "On Click" box to create a new event. Drag the Image object into the "On Click" and under the dropdown, navigate to GameObject > SetActive. This should cause a checkbox to appear below it. Check this on for one button and off for another, and make sure you have a way to tell them apart.
Now, clicking the buttons should show and hide the image.

lessons.title: Unity Tilemaps
lessons.summary: In this lesson you will learn how to use tilemaps in Unity and how to build levels with the tilemap editor.
lessons.author: Alex Li

files.name: Cobblestone (Tile)
Dirt (Tile)

figures.text: By this point, you should know how to create an object in Unity. Create a new tilemap object (under Create -> 2D Object -> Tilemap -> Rectangular)

In order to use our new tilemap, we need to add some tiles to the palette. With tilemaps, you are free to use whichever tiles you like but for this example, we will use the Minecraft cobblestone and dirt textures which you can download at the top of this page.

To create our tile palette, we first need to open the tilemap editor window. in the desktop bar, go Window -> 2D -> Tile Palette. This will open a new tab in a separate window. You can drag the “tab” section into an area next to the inspector to easily switch between the tabs.

Now to create the palette, click on the dropdown at the top that says "Create New Tile Palette". When you create a tilemap, it will ask you for a few settings. For this lesson, default settings are fine and we can just continue without changing anything.

To import a sprite into Unity, you can just drag it from your file explorer into the Unity project tab. However, since we are using pixel art for these tiles, we need to change some of the import settings. Change the following import settings Sprite mode: Single (since we are using individual sprites, not sprite sheets Pixels per unite: 16 (size of the sprite we are using)Filter mode: Point (since we are using pixel art) Compression: None (again since we are using pixel art) Click “Apply” at the bottom to save these settings. Then, simply drag the tiles into the tile palette.
To use the tile editor, simply click on the tile you want to draw with and click on the tilemap to place tiles. You can also quickly fill entire squares with tiles or erase using the editor.
To make tiles collide with/block the player, add a TilemapCollider2D to the tilemap object and it will collide just like your manually placed walls.

lessons.title: Unity Collectible Items
lessons.summary: In this lesson you will learn how to make the player collect objects. You should already have a player that can move around the scene and have simple collisions working.
lessons.author: Lindsey Li

figures.text: First, let’s make a coin object that the player can collect. After the player touches the coin, it should disappear. In this case, we want Unity to detect the collision but we don’t want the player to be blocked by the coin, so we will use Triggers.
Create a new GameObject that represents the coin. In the Inspector, add a Circle Collider 2D component. Inside the collider component, check the box that says “Is Trigger”

A trigger has the same functionality as a regular collider without the physical reaction. Turning on Is Trigger means that the object will not be solid anymore and the player can walk through it, but Unity will still detect when the player is touching the object.

There are some methods that are automatically called when an object touches the trigger, which are almost the same as the other collider methods. Add a new script to the coin object and add these methods. We want the coin to disappear as soon as the player touches it, so we will write code inside OnTriggerEnter2D.

OnTriggerEnter2D will be called when any object touches the coin, not just the player, so we need a way to identify whether the colliding object is the player. To do this, we can add the “Player” tag to the Player object in the Inspector.

We can check if the collision object is the Player by comparing the tag and then destroying the coin. Here, “gameObject” refers to the object that the script is attached to, which is the coin in this case, so Destroy(gameObject) will remove the coin from the scene.

What if we want to add many coins into the scene quickly? If we just copy pasted everything, it would take a long time to change one detail like the size of the coin. We can use Prefabs, which are templates for a GameObject that lets you easily create the same object.

To make the coin object a prefab, drag the GameObject into your project window. To make more coins, simply drag the Prefab from the project window into the hierarchy or scene. If you change any property in the coin prefab, those changes will be applied to all coins.
Now you should be able to collect coins!

lessons.title: Unity 2D Collisions
lessons.summary: In this lesson, you will learn how to make the player interact with other objects. From the last lesson, you should already have a player that can move around in a 2d scene.
lessons.author: Lindsey Li

figures.text: You can add a Rigidbody 2D to objects which will apply physics to the objects

items: There are three types of rigidbodies:
Dynamic: affected by physics, gravity, forces, used for players/enemies
Kinematic: objects that are moved using a script
Static: never moves, used for walls/platforms

figures.text: The player should already have a Rigidbody 2d component. The gravity scale should be set to 0, which means that the player won’t fall down. You should also check the box that says Freeze Rotation Z under Constraints to prevent the player from rotating about the Z axis.
Colliders allow unity to automatically handle collision detection. Both objects need to have a collider in order for a collision to happen and one of them needs a Rigidbody.

There are many types of colliders. Choose the collider that fits the shape of your object best. Usually simple shapes (boxes, circles, capsules) work the best and are the most often used.For the player, add a Box Collider 2D because it is a square shape. Always remember to choose the 2D version!You can change the size and position of the collider by pressing edit collider and directly changing it in the scene, or by changing the values in the inspector. The green outline around the object represents the collider.

Now let’s make a wall that will block the player. First, create a new 2D object (right click → 2D Object → Sprites → Square). Add a Box Collider 2D to the wall. We don’t need a Rigidbody here because the wall doesn’t move.
Now, try moving your player into the wall, it shouldn’t be able to go through.

We can also create objects that the player can push around.Make a new object with a Rigidbody 2D and Collider 2D. Remember to set the rigidbody to have gravity = 0 and freeze z rotation. Try moving the player to push the object, it should move in the same direction. You can make the object easier or harder to push by changing its mass or linear damping in the inspector.

What if we want something to happen when the player collides with an object?There are some methods we can use that are automatically called when a collision happens.OnCollisionEnter2D: called when the collision first beginsOnCollisionStay2D: called every frame while the collision is happeningOnCollisionExit2D: called when the collision ends
Create a new script for the player and add these methods. When you collide with objects in the scene, you should see messages show up in the console.

The parameter Collision2D collision has information about the collision, including the other object that the player collided with. You can access the other GameObject using collision.gameObject which allows you to access properties of the object.

lessons.title: Pixel art character design
lessons.summary: In this lesson, we will create a simple pixel art character walking.
lessons.author: Avelyn Park

figures.text: In this lesson, we will create a simple pixel art character walking.

Find or make a character that you would like to pixelate - for this lesson, we will use Frieren. Next, we will create a simple pixel character based on the model. Go to https://www.pixilart.com/, and click on start drawing.

Our artwork is drawn at 64x64 pixels because pixel art relies on low resolution to give characters their retro, simplified look. To make your artwork look crisp and sharp, upscale your final image when exporting (e.g., size 25x) rather than drawing on a larger canvas!

When creating a character, it is essential that you simplify the character as best as you can, leaving out the details and leaving only the most visible character trait. For creating a side profile, first make a simple structure of the pixel art character. This will serve as the base.

Create a new layer by clicking on the plus sign on the righthand side: think of it as a transparent sheet of film or glass stacked on top of other sheets that allow you to work on different parts of an artwork independently.
Then, we will start to add details - make sure they are simplified - cross reference the picture as you do this.

First, the hair - Frieren’s hair is very unique, and it’s one of the traits that define her character, meaning, we need to emphasize this as much as possible! Make sure you are on the different layer as you follow these steps:Start with the outline -
Then, we will color it in! - feel free to use a paint can or the pencil tool for this part.
Next, we will draw her skin - make a different layer, situate it below the hair but above the base layer - you can organize the layers using the arrow buttons in the same panel.
We start with the outline again - it can be different from the base, don’t worry if it doesn’t follow the base completely - just color in the blank parts.

At this point, we can toggle off the visibility of the base - we won’t need it anymore - click the circle on the lefthand side. This will allow the base to be turned invisible and ineffective temporarily.
Next, we will color her in. Feel free to change the color as you do this. I changed mine from pink to yellow using the paint can tool.
Now, we will start working on facial features - for the facial features, make sure you don’t get too detailed - you can edit the face as you go on.

Then we have the clothes - outline, color, all the repeating steps- make sure that this is in a different layer - sadly, if you draw in the same layer, you might face the consequence of restarting your drawing.
Lastly, we will polish things out: feel free to go back to the old layers and edit them, or make a new layer to add a little bit of details(Not too much)Polished final look with shadows:

figures.caption: Export transparently: File > export > download as png.

lessons.title: Unity Input System
lessons.summary: One or two sentences describing what a member will have built by the end.
lessons.author: Alex Li

figures.text: Move a player around the unity scene using arrow key controls

items: Click the blue "New project" button in the top right
Select "Universal 2D" as your template
Select GitHub as your version control provider
Click "Create Project"

figures.text: The Unity UI consists of a few main sections visualized by the image below

items: Scene: This is where you edit what the game looks like. Takes up most of the screen.
Hierarchy: Displays the relationships between objects located in the scene. Usually located on the left side.
Inspector: Shows an individual object in high detail. Usually located on the right side.
Project: Shows project scripts, sprites, and other imported or created components. Usually located on the bottom.
Console: Shows messages, warnings, and errors logged during playtime. Usually located on the bottom.

figures.alt: What the Unity UI looks like
figures.caption: What the Unity UI looks like

figures.text: Right click in your project tab at the bottom and select Create -> Scripting -> MonoBehaviour Script
When you first open the script, you should see something like the code shown below
MonoBehaviour is the base class used for attaching components to game objects. It includes several built in methods such as

items: Awake: Executes once when the script is loaded
Start: Executes once after Awake just before Updates start
Update: Executes once every frame while the script is enabled
FixedUpdate: Executes at fixed intervals - useful for physics
LateUpdate: Executes once every frame after Update

figures.text: For more detailed information about MonoBehaviour, check out the official Unity documentation

In order to move our player, we need to know a few factors, such as how fast we want our player to move, which player to move, and where to get the input from. Add the following fields into your script
In Awake, run GetComponent to initialize the script's reference to the object's Rigidbody2D component
The OnMove method will be called by the actual PlayerInput component.
Update the player's position in FixedUpdate
We want to create a new player GameObject to actually move. To do this, right click in your hierarchy and select 2D Object -> Sprites -> Square
You should now have a new square in the scene. To add the script to this object, select it and in the inspector, click "Add Component". Search for your script and add it.
You should see a box with the label "Move Speed" under the script in inspector. The speed can be changed by adjusting this number without modifying the original script.
A Rigidbody2D component should have also been added to your player. Make sure to set "Gravity Scale" to 0 in order for your inputs to work correctly
Add the "PlayerInput" component to your GameObject. Configure it as follows

items: Default scheme: Keyboard & Mouse
Default map: Player
Camera: Main Camera (click the circle and select "Main Camera")
Behaviour: Invoke Unity Events

figures.text: To connect your script with the PlayerInput component, expand Events -> Player
Under Move click the plus sign to create a new binding. Attach your Player object by dragging it in from the hierarchy. In the dropdown on the right, select PlayerMovement -> OnMove
Click the play button on the top bar to enter play mode and test your script. You should be able to move the square around using WASD controls
